subject: Full likelihood approach: the likelihood component pertaining to the detection model with continuous coviarates & handling nested covariates

messages.author: b480b89888b88e0e
messages.subject: Full likelihood approach: the likelihood component pertaining to the detection model with continuous coviarates & handling nested covariates
parts:
Hello,

We've been working on Oedekoven (2020)'s code for a full likelihood approach to fit a half-normal detection function to line transect data. For our detection model we're using the continous covariates of forbs height (F_HT_MDN) and cover (F_CVR_MDN) median values per transect, whereas for our count model we're using the continous covariates of plot age (OP_AGE) and Julian date (JDctr). However, I've a couple of questions regading the ml.log.lik function:
  1. In part 2, how do I handle continous covariates as opposed to factorial covariates (as shown in the example)? Also, how do I handle more than one covariate here?
    • Here's the code adapted to our data:
        # Part 2
        # the likelihood component pertaining to the detection model
        # calculating the f(y) for each observed distances
        le<-nrow(datax$dis.object)
        fe<-numeric(le)
        allf.ht<-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN))
        dis.f.ht<-match(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN,allf.ht)
        allf.cvr<-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN))
        dis.f.cvr<-match(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN,allf.cvr)
        # the sigma(z) for each detection
        allscale<-exp(scale.int+sig.f.ht[dis.f.ht]+sig.f.cvr[dis.f.cvr])
    • The issue appears to be in the allscale line, where everything shows as NA. I reckon this is due to the handling of continous as opposed to categorical data.
  2. Right now we're using OP_AGE as a continous covariate (0 to 18, where 0 represents active plots, and 18 correspond to unmodified habitat, whereas all inbetween are fallow lands of varous ages since abandonment), but we're interested in implementing a nested design where a continous covariate (age) is nested inside a factor covariate. Is this possible?
Thanks in advance for the help.

messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Full likelihood approach: the likelihood component pertaining to the detection model with continuous coviarates & handling nested covariates
parts:
Hi Elipaleth,  

Great you are using the code and sorry to hear you had trouble making it work for your own study.  

In general, using a continuous covariate should be easier than a factor covariate and you can simply set up multiple continuous, multiple factor or a combination of both.  

Here is an example of how you would set up the scale for two continuous covariates. Remember you might have to force R to look at your variable as a numeric variable by using e.g. as.numeric(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN).  

# you don’t need these lines anymore 

#allf.ht<-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN)) 

#  dis.f.ht<-match(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN,allf.ht) 

#  allf.cvr<-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN)) 

#  dis.f.cvr<-match(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN,allf.cvr)
# the sigma(z) for each detection

allscale<-exp(scale.int+sig.f.ht*datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN )+sig.f.cvr*datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN 

Now, sig.f.ht and sig.f.cvr are each a single coefficient associated with their respective variables. 

I am not sure I follow your second question. Do you mean that age might have a different effect depending on the type of habitat? If that is the case, here is an example of how you might set this up. Let’s say habitat is a factor covariate and age is a continuous covariate. You could use an interaction term in the model. This will give you different slope coefficients for age for each habitat (in addition to the coefficients for each habitat). If you are interested in setting up such an interaction term for one of your models, it gets a bit complicated but I can try to help you work this out if you wish.  

Hope this helps. Cheers, Cornelia

parts:
Dear Eliphaleth,

Great to hear you got it working.

Regarding your second question: please have a look at the code we published along with the JAPPL paper (see the code for the Integrated Approach in Appendix 1 here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.12065)
You will see code for models which don't have any covariate in the glmm part (models 1-4) and a model which has continuous (day) and factor covariates (type and state) in the glmm part (model 9). Please compare e.g. models 4 and 9 to see the difference between including (model 9) or not including (model 4) covariates in the glmm part.

Regarding your third question: I'll modify some lines from our paper to illustrate the example. Remember that if you have e.g. continuous day and factor state as covariates in your glmm model (e.g. as in model 9 - in addition to factor type), the part of the code pertaining to these two covariates is (see e.g. line 357 in our published code I referred to above):

+ Day[ik,tk]*day + st[State[ik,1]]

Here, 'day' is a single value coefficient for the continuous effect of Day and state is a vector of length 8. If I was interested in an interaction between state and Day, the code would change to:

+ Day[ik,tk]*day + st[State[ik,1]] + Day[ik,tk]*day.int[State[ik,1]]

where day.int would be a vector of 8 and model the varying effects of Day within the different states. Remember that the top of the likelihood function would need to be altered as well in order to include the extra parameters that require estimation:

model9.log.lik.fct <- function(p){
sigma <- p[1:9]
int <- p[10]
typ <- p[11]
day <- p[12]
st <- c(0, p[13:20])
day.int <- c(0, p[21:28])
std.ran <- exp(p[29])

I hope this helps and you will be able to modify this according to your needs.

Best wishes, Cornelia
